query: High-entropy alloys contain five or more elements at 5–35 at% each, generally with comparable atomic radii. Refractory and nickel-based high-entropy alloys have demonstrated elevated-temperature mechanical properties comparable to titanium- and nickel-based alloys used in extreme environments because of their heat resistance and specific strength. However, prior investigations have mainly treated titanium and nickel as additions, leaving alloys in which both are primary constituents unexplored. Subject to the stated compositional definition, what single testable intervention hypothesis could improve the elevated-temperature mechanical properties of a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy relative to the same material without the intervention? Specify the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted relative outcome, composition and operating boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment with explicit results that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding approximately 2 at% tungsten into a titanium‐ and nickel‐primary high-entropy alloy will improve its elevated-temperature mechanical properties relative to the same alloy without tungsten.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy in which titanium and nickel are the primary constituents (e.g., roughly equal high at% of Ti and Ni along with other elements that meet the 5–35 at% requirement) in an as-cast or conventionally processed state.
generation.intervention: Introduce roughly 2 at% tungsten into the alloy composition during melting/alloying.
generation.conditions: Evaluated under high-temperature conditions (e.g., tensile and creep tests at around 650°C) within the compositional limits of high-entropy alloys.
generation.structural_mediator: W tungsten atoms are expected to provide increased lattice distortion and act as strong solid-solution strengtheners. Their presence may promote the formation or stabilization of fine precipitates that hinder grain boundary migration/dislocation mobility.
generation.mechanism: The tungsten addition is predicted to increase the resistance to dislocation motion and creep deformation by introducing localized lattice strain and enhancing solid solution as well as potential precipitate strengthening effects. These changes could reduce dislocation mobility and mitigate grain boundary sliding that typically degrades high-temperature performance.
generation.predicted_outcome: The tungsten-doped alloy will exhibit higher yield strength at 650°C, improved creep rupture life, and potentially more uniform plastic deformation compared to the baseline alloy lacking tungsten.
generation.baseline: The titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy without any tungsten addition.
generation.boundary: The intervention is applicable as long as the overall alloy composition adheres to the high-entropy alloy criteria (each major element in the range of approximately 5–35 at%), with testing performed at elevated temperatures (near 650°C) where high-temperature mechanical properties are critical.
generation.uncertainty: While prior studies on refractory and nickel-based HEAs suggest improvements from similar strengthening mechanisms, the exact magnitude of improvement and the possible interactions with other alloying elements in the Ti-Ni primary matrix remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of samples: one with the baseline titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy composition and another with the same composition but with an additional 2 at% tungsten. Process the materials using identical melting and heat-treatment procedures. Subject both sets of samples to elevated-temperature mechanical testing (e.g., tensile tests and creep tests at 650°C).
measurements: Creep rupture life under a constant load at 650°C
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the tungsten-added alloy does not show a statistically significant improvement (e.g., >10% increase in yield strength and >50% longer creep rupture life) over the baseline alloy under identical high-temperature conditions, or if it exhibits deteriorated ductility or premature failure, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: ABSTRACTIn this study, tensile and creep deformation of a high-entropy alloy processed by selective laser melting (SLM) has been investigated; hot ductility drop was identified at first, and the loss of ductility at elevated temperature was associated with intergranular fracture. By modifying the grain boundary morphology from straight to serration, the hot ductility drop issue has been resolved successfully. The serrated grain boundary could be achieved by reducing the cooling rate of solution heat treatment, which allowed the coarsening of L12 structured γ′ precipitates to interfere with mobile grain boundaries, resulting in undulation of the grain boundary morphology. Tensile and creep tests at 650°C were conducted, and serrated grain boundary could render a significant increase in tensile fracture strain and creep rupture life by a factor of 3.5 and 400, respectively. Detailed microstructure analysis has indicated that serrated grain boundary could distribute strains more evenly than that of straight morphology. This work has demonstrated that a simple post heat treatment could induce SEGB in a HEA fabricated by SLM. The serrations on grain boundary in HT-samples were attributed to the blocky irregular shaped γ′ precipitates formed during the slow cooling process, and they could pin the mobile grain boundaries as well as restricting grain growth, this phenomenon is known as the Zener drag effect []. The drag force from the coarse precipitates would hinder the migration of grain boundary, while those free from the precipitates could break free around the precipitates and resulted in serrated morphology (Figure 4(c)). The inhibition of grain growth from coarse precipitates explained why HT-2 sample possessed a smaller grain size than that of HT-1 sample. The difference in tensile yield strength between HT-1 and HT-2 at 25°C and 650°C could be associated with the size of γ′ precipitates. According to Jackson – Reed model [], the strengthening contribution of γ′ precipitate could be inverse proportional to the average radius of the precipitate.
